text: Every package you've built in this course points at something specific to your machine — a connection string, a file path. This lesson is about what happens the moment that package has to run somewhere else entirely.

A package that's hard-coded for your development machine is wrong the moment it deploys to a test server, and wrong again in production. Package Configurations are Integration Services' original answer — a mechanism that overrides specific package properties from an external source every time the package starts, without touching the package file itself. That override can come from one of five places: an XML configuration file, an environment variable, a registry entry, a parent package variable, or a SQL Server table. The most common by far is an XML file, often set up indirectly — an environment variable that just holds the file's location, so even that can move between servers freely. Setting one up walks you through the Package Configuration Wizard: enable package configurations from the SSIS menu, choose a configuration type, point it at a location, and then, on the key step, expand the object tree and check exactly which properties — a connection manager's connection string, a variable's value — this configuration is allowed to override. Finish the wizard, and from then on, every run reads that external source first and overwrites the matching properties before a single task executes.

One important caveat: configurations only work with the legacy Package Deployment Model. If you're on the Project Deployment Model, you already have the modern replacement — the Parameters you learned back in Chapter 5. Next lesson, we look at a different kind of composition entirely: master and child packages calling each other through the Execute Package Task.
